links.note: 101 says that for help given without any prior help (செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி) even earth and heaven are hardly a match (ஆற்றல் அரிது). 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா) and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange (என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ). The same verb ஆற்று marks both: one verse looks from the receiver who cannot repay, the other from the giver who does not ask to be repaid.

Both open with செய்யாமல், 'without (the other) having done anything first'. 101 applies it to help: unprompted help is beyond repayment. 313 applies it to hatred: even toward those who hate you though you did nothing (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), doing hurt brings sorrow with no escape. Read together, the unprovoked good creates a boundless debt while the unprovoked wrong still gives no licence to retaliate.

102 says help done at the time of need (காலத்தினால் செய்த நன்றி), though small, is greater than the earth. 788 makes that timeliness the definition of friendship: it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand going to a slipping garment. 102 values the help by its moment; 788 says what kind of helper acts in that moment.

103 praises help from those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்), calling its good greater than the sea. 813 uses the same weighing verb for the opposite case: friends who weigh what they will get (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) are put level with thieves. The pair shows the book judging help and friendship by one test, whether the giver was calculating.

103 sets apart help given without weighing its return (பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி). 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving, and everything else has the nature of a loan expecting return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீரது). Both separate real help from exchange, 103 from the side of gratitude and 221 from the side of the giver.

The two verses share a frame almost word for word: தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர். In 104 those who understand its fruit (பயன்தெரிவார்) take a millet-sized good done to them as palmyra-sized; in 433 those ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a millet-sized fault of their own as palmyra-sized. The same magnifying habit is recommended for others' kindness and for one's own faults.

104 uses millet and palmyra (தினைத்துணை, பனைத்துணை) for how a small good should be valued. 1282, a lover's speech in the Book of Love, reuses the pair: when love comes full as a palmyra (பனைத்துணையும் காமம் நிறைய வரின்) there should be not even a millet of sulking (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை). The measure-pair moves from ethics to love, there contrasting two quantities where 104 converts one into the other.

104 says a millet of good is taken as a palmyra by those who know its worth. 109 says even harm like killing (கொன்றன்ன இன்னா) vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 109: because the small good is held as large, that one good can cancel the later harm.

105 says help is not bounded by the help itself; its measure is the worth of the one helped (செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து). 87 says the fruit of hospitality has no fixed size; it is as great as the guest (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). Both verses move the measure of an act of giving from the gift to the character of the person who receives it.

Both verses use the phrase மாசற்றார் கேண்மை, the bond of the stainless: 106 says do not forget it (மறவற்க), 800 says keep close to it (மருவுக). Each then adds a second command about a kind of friend, 106 never to abandon those who were a support in distress, 800 to drop the unsuitable (ஒப்பிலார்) even at a cost. The chapter on choosing friends repeats the gratitude chapter's rule and supplies its other half, whom to leave.

106 commands: do not abandon (துறவற்க) the friendship of those who were a support in distress. 806 states it as a description: those who keep within the bounds will not abandon (துறவார்) the tie of long-standing friends even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்). The same verb is used in both, with the direction reversed: 106 is loyalty owed for help received in one's own trouble, 806 loyalty kept when trouble comes.

107 says people will remember (உள்ளுவர்) through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their distress. 799 says the bond with those who abandoned one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when thought of (உள்ளினும்) at the hour of death. Both are about how conduct in another's hard time is remembered: the helper for lives to come, the deserter up to the last moment.

107 says the friendship of one who removed one's distress is remembered through seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்). 398 says learning gained in one birth (ஒருமைக்கண்) is a protection through seven (எழுமையும்). The seven-birth span is the book's figure for what outlasts a single life, used here for a debt of gratitude and there for learning.

108 says it is good to forget what is not good that very day (நன்றல்லது அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று). 152 says bear with a wrong, and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). Both put forgetting an injury above merely tolerating it; 108 pairs it with the opposite duty of never forgetting a good.

108 says a wrong done to you should be forgotten that very day (அன்றே மறப்பது). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day (அன்றே ஒழிய விடல்). The shared அன்றே gives both the same urgency: neither a grievance nor an unfair gain is to be kept overnight.

109 says that even harm like killing disappears when one recalls a single good the person once did (அவர் செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ள). 807 says those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when the friend does ruinous things (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). Both have the same 'even if they do grave harm' (செயினும்) clause; what outweighs the harm is a remembered favour in one and long affection in the other.

110 says those who kill any good may have an escape (உய்வுண்டாம்), but there is none for one who kills a good done to him (செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு). 207 has the same shape: those who incur any enmity (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும்) escape (உய்வர்), but the enmity of one's deeds follows and kills. Both use 'everything else can be survived' to single out one thing, ingratitude in 110 and evil deeds in general in 207.

110 says there is escape (உய்வுண்டாம்) for other wrongs but none (உய்வில்லை) for killing gratitude. 896 says one burned by fire may survive (உய்வுண்டாம்), but those who go on offending the great will not (உய்யார்). The same உய்வு formula marks what each chapter treats as its unforgivable offence, so a reader should take 'only this has no escape' as the book's way of stressing gravity and not as a strict ranking.

111 says the virtue called தகுதி is good if one keeps to what is due in each case (பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுக); Parimelazhagar takes பகுதி as enemy, stranger and friend. 541 defines a king's justice (முறை) as inquiring, showing favour to no one (யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது) and acting after consideration. The householder's impartiality of 111 reappears as the procedure of the ruler's court.

111 asks that fairness be kept alike across the divisions of people, on Parimelazhagar's reading toward enemy, stranger and friend. 528 says a king should not look on all in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) but according to rank or merit (வரிசையா நோக்கின்), and many will then stay by him. Together they show that impartiality in 111 does not mean identical treatment: one may not favour by relationship, but one should distinguish by desert.

112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to his descendants. 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 thus limits 112 to the usual course of things; Parimelazhagar explains the exceptions by deeds of earlier births.

112 says a fair person's wealth is a support to his posterity (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 states the reverse: if one covets others' goods without fairness (நடுவின்றி), the family perishes (குடிபொன்றி) and guilt comes at once. Both tie நடுவு to what happens to one's line, 112 as promise and 171 as warning.

112 says the wealth of the fair person does not decay and secures those who come after (எச்சம்). 44 says that if a household fears blame and shares its food, its line never fails (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்); Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. Both promise continuity of the family to blameless livelihood, with 44 adding sharing as a condition.

113 says to give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்), even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 328 says that, however great the gain that brings good (நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும்), gain that comes by killing (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம்) is lowest to the worthy. The same concession, 'even if it is good and large', is refused in both; only the forbidden means differs.

113 says to abandon gain got by departing from fairness even if it brings good. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth gained by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 657 names the price that 113 leaves unstated: giving up such gain may mean poverty, and the book accepts that.

114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen by their எச்சம், what they leave behind; Parimelazhagar takes this as having or lacking good children. 456 says those pure of mind have a good எச்சம் (எச்சம் நன்றாகும்), which he again reads as offspring. The two run the same link in opposite directions: 456 from character to legacy, 114 from legacy back to character.

114 makes எச்சம் the evidence of whether someone was fair. 238 speaks of 'the எச்சம் called renown' (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்) and calls it a disgrace not to leave it. 238 supports reading the legacy in 114 as reputation, which is how Kalaignar takes it, against Parimelazhagar's reading of children.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life (கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல), and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. 379 asks why those who take good as good when it comes grieve when the opposite comes (அன்றாங்கால் அல்லற்படுவது எவன்). Both ask for the same response to gain and loss; Parimelazhagar grounds both in the working of past deeds.

115 says loss and increase both occur, and the worthy keep the heart from bending because of them. 169 gives the hard case: the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright are ruined (செவ்வியான் கேடு), which calls for reflection. 169 shows the situation in which 115's advice is tested, when fortune seems to reward bending.

115 and 118 end with the same line, கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி, 'not bending is the ornament of the worthy'. In 115 the bending is of the heart under loss and gain (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை); in 118 it is leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like a balance. The repetition joins two sides of நடுவு: steadiness under one's own fortunes and impartiality between others.

116 says that if one's heart leaves fairness and does wrong (நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்), one should know 'I will perish' (கெடுவல்யான்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin even by a lapse, for அறம் will plot the plotter's ruin (சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both say that harm intended for others returns as one's own ruin; 116 makes it the wrongdoer's own knowledge, 204 gives the agent as அறம்.

116 locates the departure from fairness in the heart (தன் நெஞ்சம்), and Parimelazhagar reads செயின் as covering even the thought of doing wrong. 282 says outright that merely thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong. 282 supports that reading of 116: the fault begins with the intention, before any act.

117 says the world (உலகம்) will not count as ruin the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even if they have every good quality'. They conflict if உலகம் in 117 means people in general; Parimelazhagar avoids this by reading உலகம் there as the high-minded (உயர்ந்தோர்).

117 says the low state of a person who stands fair is not held to be ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது). 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called சால்பு. Both deny that poverty lowers a person of character; 117 says it for fairness in particular, 988 for worth as a whole.

118 compares the worthy to the balance beam (சீர்தூக்கும் கோல்) that levels itself and then weighs, not leaning to a side (கோடாமை). 546 says it is the king's sceptre (கோல்), not his spear, that gives victory, if it does not bend (கோடாது). கோல் and கோடுதல் carry the same idea in both: the weighing beam of the private person and the sceptre of the ruler are good only while straight.

118 describes a balance that first makes itself level (சமன்செய்து) and then weighs (சீர்தூக்கும்). 561 says a king is one who examines a case fittingly (தக்காங்கு நாடி) and punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது); Parimelazhagar glosses the examining as done 'standing in the middle' (நடுவாக நின்று). The two steps of the scale, being level and then measuring, match the two steps of just punishment.

119 says rectitude is the absence of crookedness in speech (சொற்கோட்டம்), provided there is none within (உட்கோட்டம்). 279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute (யாழ்கோடு) is good, so judge people by what their deeds do. Both use straight and bent to separate appearance from substance: 119 will not take straight words as proof without a straight mind, and 279 will not take outward shape as proof at all.

119 makes unbent speech count as rectitude only if the mind too is unbent (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்). 295 praises one who speaks truth together with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity and give. Both attach the same condition to good speech, agreement between word and mind, in the fields of fairness and of truthfulness.

120 says true trade for traders is to look after others' things as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல்). 315 asks what use understanding is if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). The same 'as one's own' (தம்போல்) test is applied to goods in the market and to suffering in the chapter on not hurting.

120 asks traders to care for what belongs to others as for what is theirs (பிறவும் தமபோல் பேணி). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame at others' blame and their own (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame; Parimelazhagar reads this as weighing the two alike. Both define a virtue, fairness in one and shame in the other, by removing the difference between oneself and others.
